root: ^He came back to himself the way a dream ended: all at once, and leaving nothing behind.

^The first thing he knew was ash. Fine and pale as ground bone, it clung to his cloak, his hair, the cold space between his fingers, a finger's depth on every flat surface and deeper in the hollows. The air tasted like old fire and something older than fire, metal and memory, sharp enough to sting but too worn to wound.

^Then he wasn't. His body made the decision before he did, propping itself upright with the automatic dignity of something that had survived worse and intended to keep surviving. His arms shook with the effort. He let them. Shaking was information. Shaking meant he was here.
^He sat in the ash and looked at the world.

^The sky was lavender-gray and infinite, neither day nor night. A held breath that had forgotten how to release. No sun, no stars, no shadow to tell him which direction was worth walking in. The scorched trees ringing the hollow stood stripped of everything that had once made them particular, their blackened branches reaching upward like people who had stopped mid-sentence and never found their way back to the point. No wind moved them. No birdsong broke the stillness. The ash fell as though it had been asked very politely to keep the noise down.

^He patted himself down. His cloak was worn soft with use but still committed to its purpose. His boots were practical, worn at the heels, resoled at least once, the boots of someone who walked more than they sat and was always slightly underprepared for the conditions they walked into. His gloves were mismatched. One dark gray, one darker, stitched unevenly along the thumb where the original seam had given out, the repair made quickly and from memory, because the stitching was functionally sound and executed by someone who had done it before without being able to see the original.

^When he pulled them off, his fingers were ink-stained. The kind that had been washed many times and declined to leave, faded into the whorls of his fingerprints, settled into the creases of his knuckles. His right index finger had a callus on the side that came from holding something for long periods. A pen. A piece of charcoal.
^Someone who worked with words, those hands said. Someone who worried at them the way other people worried at loose threads.
^He had absolutely no idea who that person was.
^The hands were more forthcoming than the mind. It meant the person was still in there somewhere, encoded into muscle and callus and old ink, waiting for the rest of him to catch up.
^He was here. He had been elsewhere and now he was here, and between those two facts was a space so complete that looking directly at it made something behind his eyes hurt.
^"Who am I?" he said aloud. Not because he expected an answer. Because the question was there and the silence seemed to expect something from him.
^The wind didn't answer. But it paused.

^He stood. His legs had opinions. His knees made sounds knees weren't designed to make. He managed upright anyway, swayed once, found his footing in the ash, it gave slightly under his weight, whispering, and looked out at the nothing surrounding him in every direction.

^The hollow was perhaps thirty paces across. Far to what he was arbitrarily deciding was north, the rim rose slightly before dropping away into more gray. To the south, scorched trees stood close enough together to imply they had once been a forest and still hadn't quite accepted what had happened to it.
^"Well," he said. "One way's as good as any other."

^He chose north, on the theory that high ground was useful and a decision made for a bad reason was still better than no decision at all. He picked up the cloak's hem and walked. The ash came to mid-shin in the drifts and shallowed to fine grit on the exposed stone between them, and walking was the kind of work that told you, after ten minutes, exactly which muscles had been still too long.

^The landscape shifted around its own indifference as he moved. A slope appeared where none had been visible from the hollow, rising gradually enough that he was halfway up before he understood what he was doing. Stone pushed through the ash in jagged lines, darker than the surrounding gray, veined with something pale that caught what little light existed and held it without warmth.

notice_hands: ^He walked, and his hands walked with him, and eventually he looked at them.

^The gloves were mismatched. He'd known that already, in the cursory way of someone cataloguing damage before deciding whether to care about it. But he stopped caring about the gloves and started caring about what was underneath: the ink. Old enough that washing hadn't moved it, settled into his fingerprints and the creases of his knuckles as if it had applied for permanent residency and been approved some time ago. His right index finger had a callus on the side, built up by something held for long hours, something narrow and consistent. A pen. A piece of charcoal, possibly.
^He turned his hands over. Then back.

^Someone who worked with words, the hands said, in the particular way that hands communicated things the mind had no access to. Someone who came back to the same problem repeatedly and kept trying different arrangements of it.
^He looked at the ink for a while. Tried to feel something recognizable.

^Nothing arrived. The ink knew who he was. He did not, yet, and the ink wasn't explaining itself, only stating the fact of its presence with the patience of a thing that had been doing this for years and expected to keep doing it.
^He tucked his hands back into his cloak and walked.
notice_trees: ^He walked, and the trees walked with him, in the sense that they were always at the edge of things, always just present enough to register.
^He stopped at one of the fallen ones.

^It had been enormous. Wider than he was tall, its bark long stripped to silver-gray, its rings visible in the exposed cross-section and too numerous to count before the light made counting impossible. He put his hand against the wood as he passed, without quite deciding to. It was dry. Absolutely cold. It had been dead for a very long time, and whatever had killed it had been thorough.
^Whatever had killed it had killed everything else in the same moment.

^He stood with that thought for exactly as long as it took to understand that following it would not help him and might stop him entirely. He was aware that not following a thought was not the same as the thought being wrong. He was also aware that being stopped was a worse outcome than proceeding with incomplete information, and that he had no other kind.
^The tree remained exactly as dead as it had been. He had not worsened anything by leaving it there.
the_displacement: ^Not loudly, and not with any of the drama the word crack usually implied. It simply bent, the way heat bent light above stone in summer, except there was no heat here, just the gray ash-plain doing its impression of endlessness. Behind him, from the exact spot he had just left, a distortion rippled upward, a shimmer, a stutter, space briefly reconsidering its relationship with staying still. It lifted the ash around it in a slow impossible spiral, particles rising against the absent wind, catching the flat light and turning it into something almost beautiful before settling back into nothing.
^He was no longer standing in that spot.

^He was several paces away, facing back the way he had come, heart hammering with a speed disproportionate to anything he could explain. His palms were alive with something caught between pain and electricity. He had no memory of moving.
^He looked at his hands. At the place he had been standing. Back at his hands.

^No answer. The shimmer faded. The ash settled. The world resumed its position on the matter of complete indifference to his circumstances. He was aware, standing very still, that the absence of a second occurrence was not the same as the inability to produce one.
^He tucked his hands into his cloak and kept walking.

^He walked until the land offered shelter without being asked. A ring of low stones in a shallow depression, eight or nine of them, each about knee-height, uncarved but placed with the considered spacing of something arranged rather than accumulated. The ground inside was firmer, the ash swept thinner. It felt quieter inside the ring, not in volume but in intention, as though the space had been designated for something and still held that shape, even after whatever it had been designated for was gone.
^He sat with his back against one of the stones and let his legs register their formal objections and then go quiet.
let_move: ^His hand moved before he'd decided it would.

^It was already reaching, already navigating the interior of his cloak with a purposefulness his mind had not signed off on, and he watched it do this with the particular feeling of someone realizing, mid-observation, that they have been operating on more than one level for quite some time.

^This was not nothing, as decisions went. He wasn't sure he trusted the body entirely. But it had gotten him upright when upright was necessary and walking when walking was the only available answer, and it seemed, in the absence of anything the mind could offer, the appropriate authority to defer to. The body had context he didn't. He was willing to admit that.
^His hand found something in the interior fold of the cloak and stopped.
stop_first: ^His hand had moved before he'd decided it would.

^Not from suspicion, exactly. More from the feeling that if someone was going to reach inside his own cloak, it should probably be him making that choice and not some older version of himself conducting business from the other side of a door he couldn't open. He sat with the wanting-to-reach for a breath. Two. Long enough to establish that he was, at least nominally, the one in charge here.
^Then his hand moved again, slower this time. Deliberate. He let it.

^The difference was small. He suspected it mattered anyway. He couldn't have explained why, only that something in him felt it was important to have paused — that the pause was not the same as resistance, only the difference between following and choosing to follow, which were the same direction but not the same thing.
^His hand found something in the interior fold of the cloak and stopped.
the_charcoal: ^The first was a piece of charcoal. Small, worn nearly to nothing, rounded by long use to the shape that fitted his grip. It fit into his fingers with the rightness of a thing that had been there many times before. It was very nearly used up. Whatever it had been writing, it had been writing a lot of it.

^The smell of it, when he brought it close, opened something. Not a memory. The shape where a memory had been, smoke and intention, the smell of words in progress, the mental atmosphere of working something out on paper at a late hour. His hands knew this smell the way hands knew the weight of familiar tools. His mind offered nothing.

^The second object was parchment. A small square, folded twice, the edges fragile with age and something that might have been heat damage, not burned, spared from burning, the way things were sometimes spared from the thing that took everything else. He unfolded it carefully.

^He stared at it for a while. The blankness was not nothing. It was expectant, the way a page held empty for the right moment felt different from one that had simply never been written on. He knew this immediately and could not have explained why.
^He held the charcoal over the page.

^The cold pressed patiently inward. Below his ribs, there was a hollow. Not a wound. An absence. The shape of something removed very carefully from the center of him, long ago, by someone who had known what they were doing. He was only noticing it now because the surrounding noise had been stripped away and there was nothing left to fill the space it occupied.

^He pressed his forehead against the parchment. The texture caught against his skin, dry and fragile and real, the most real thing he had touched since waking. He stayed there, breathing, letting the cold be cold and the hollow be hollow.

^[i]Please[/i], he thought, to no one in particular, to the listening quality of the quiet that had been following him since he woke, to whatever had left charcoal and parchment in a cloak on a person with no name in the middle of a world that had stopped. [i]I don't want to be alone.[/i]
^He didn't know if it would help. He meant it regardless.

^He didn't decide to write. He didn't choose the words. His hand moved with the certainty of something that had been waiting for permission and had finally, after a long time of waiting, received it. It pressed the charcoal to the parchment and left behind six words:

^He looked at what he had written. He turned it over in his mind the way you turned over something found on the ground, checking it from different angles. The words were his, his hand had written them. He didn't know what they meant. He was reasonably certain he hadn't known them a moment before. But looking at them now they had the quality of truth that didn't announce itself, the quiet kind, the kind that simply settled into place the way a key settled into the right lock: not loudly, not dramatically, just yes. This.
^Something in him released. Not much. A fraction of something. Just enough to breathe differently.
^He folded the parchment and put it back in the pocket he hadn't known was there.
^That night, if night was the word for a sky that continued to refuse commitment to any particular time of day, he dreamed.

^He stood in a corridor carved from stone that generated its own dim light, warm-toned and sourceless, as though the stone remembered being warmer and was trying to get back there. The corridor stretched in both directions without visible end. Above it, instead of a ceiling, the sky arched close, stars crowded together and very bright, so low they seemed to hum, positioned with an insistence that was almost right, almost what stars were supposed to do, with a fraction of wrongness that registered before it could be identified.

^Doors lined the walls. Dozens of them, no two alike. Some were carved with intricate spirals that shifted when he looked at them sideways. Others were plain as slate, without ornament or handle. One had a crack running from top to bottom, and from the crack light pressed outward, the light of something contained that wanted more room. Another door flickered at its edges, uncertain whether it wanted to remain a door or become something else.
^He walked. The corridor seemed to have an opinion about which way, and his feet agreed without consulting him.

^The stone underfoot shifted faintly with each step, not physically but tonally, a soft chord that changed as he moved, the corridor tuning itself to his pace the way a good room tuned itself to a speaker's voice.
^Linger at one of the carved-spiral doors first.
door_handle: ^He stopped at a door with no handle.

^Smooth stone, no carving, no marking of any kind. No indication, from any observable quality of the door, that it was anything other than a section of wall that had made different choices. He almost walked past it. Something made him not.
^He stood in front of it for a moment. Raised his hand.

^The stone was warm before his palm arrived. He registered this and pressed on anyway, his palm flat against the surface, and from the other side — not through the door, through the stone itself — something met him there.
^Recognition moved through the door in both directions at once.

^He didn't have a name for what he was recognizing. That was all right. Names were a later problem. The recognition was enough, for now: the sense of something arranging itself toward him the way a sound arranged itself toward an ear, not arriving so much as finally being heard. He stayed still with his hand against the warm stone for what might have been one breath or several.
^Then the door opened. Inward. Without being asked.
^The dream shifted. He let it take him.
door_spiral: ^He stopped at one of the carved doors.

^Spirals, intricate and layered, shifting slightly when he looked at them sideways, the way things shifted in dreams when you tried to look directly. He wasn't sure if they were moving or if he was. He lifted his hand toward the surface.
^Something said, very quietly and without elaboration: not yours.
^He wasn't sure if it was a sound or a thought or some third category of information that didn't have a name in the waking world. He waited to see if it elaborated. It didn't. He lowered his hand.

^There was a door with no handle further along the corridor, set slightly apart from the others, smooth stone with no carving, no marking, and warm from several feet away. He stopped in front of it. Pressed his palm flat against the surface.
^From the other side, something met him there.
^Recognition moved through the door in both directions at once, and the door opened before he'd decided what to do about that, and the dream shifted, and he let it take him.
the_recognition: ^There was no room. Only presence, the kind that occupied space the way music occupied a room, not visibly, not with any surface you could point to, but completely, changing the nature of the air it inhabited.

^A tone. Low and deep and slow, moving through him like a chord struck inside a building made of years, not heard so much as known, the way you knew a sound you had been hearing so long it had become part of the background and you only noticed it when it stopped.

^Then another. Higher. Lighter. Moving toward him the way a reflection moved, the shape of something he hadn't known he had been carrying, shown back to him from an angle he couldn't have found alone.
^The two tones met inside him, not around him.

^He didn't see a face. He felt the shape of one. Familiar in the way of people you have not yet met but already know, somehow, without evidence, without logic, that you will love. The kind of knowing that lives in the body rather than the mind. The kind that doesn't argue.
^The tone swelled gently in response. Not an answer. An acknowledgment. The difference mattered.
^From somewhere below his ribs, without permission or intention, a word surfaced:

^He didn't know what it meant, whether it was a name or a place or something that didn't have a category yet. He only knew that he missed it, immediately and completely, the way you missed something you hadn't known you'd had until the moment you understood it was gone. A loss that had been there all along, waiting for him to be quiet enough to feel it.
^The corridor shifted. Something changed in the dream, a turning, a door closing behind him without sound. The stars above moved slightly, or he moved beneath them.
^The ash-world was unchanged. Cold. Pale. Patient.

^He sat with the dream for a moment. The details were already dissolving the way dreams did, leaving only the residue of feeling: something known, something missed, something that had been waiting a very long time for him specifically. He let it settle alongside the hollow beneath his ribs and the ink on his fingers and the six words on the parchment, in the place where he was keeping things that didn't have frames yet.
^He had put the parchment away before sleeping. His hand had found it again in the dark, the way hands found familiar objects without being asked.

^It hadn't been visible before, or perhaps he hadn't seen it, which were not quite the same thing. Faint and golden, spiral-shaped, etched not into his skin but beneath it, as though it had always been present and had simply decided that now was the correct moment to stop being subtle about it. He looked at it for a long time.
^He drew a sharp breath. His teeth ached with it.

^The glyph pulsed again. A vibration moved through the ground beneath him, small and precise, traveling outward through the stone beneath the ash, dusting the fine powder from the surfaces around him. The disturbance followed lines in the stone, not random but a geometry, barely visible beneath the ash, worn to near-nothing but present. Somewhere below, deeper than the stone, something stirred. Not with threat. Not with urgency.
^He stood. Brushed ash from his cloak with hands that had stopped trembling sometime during the night. Looked out at the hills beyond the hollow's rim.

^A shimmer, at the furthest limit of the flat light. Not quite light, not quite heat, something more like the air remembering a shape it had once been taught, practicing it quietly in the hope that someone might eventually come along who needed it.
^The glyph warmed. The shimmer intensified, not brighter but more present, the way a sound became more present when you finally turned your attention toward it.

^His body knew, the way it had known to stand up and the way his hand had known what to write, that something was waiting for him at the end of this. Something that had been waiting for exactly as long as it took him to arrive, not with urgency, but with the settled patience of something that had arranged itself around a fixed point and simply continued to be arranged, through everything, until the point returned.

^He followed the shimmer through the ash and the silence and the cold. Past the hollow where he had slept, past the ring of patient stones. Past the place where the air had reconsidered itself, where the last traces of his inexplicable not-quite-displacement still faintly scattered the ash into patterns that didn't follow any wind. Past the fallen tree with its uncountable rings, past the stone that rose through the ash like an argument.
^Through the gray. Toward the hills. Toward whatever the hills were keeping.

^Behind him, for just a moment, one breath, two, the ash in his footprints glimmered. Green-veined, faintly luminous, like something beneath the surface noticing his passage and finding it, against all available evidence, worth noticing.
chapter_two_start: ^It didn't pull. It didn't urge. It simply moved, and he followed, because there was nothing else in this world pointing at anything.

^The ash had thinned. Beneath his boots, the gray dust surrendered to darker soil, not damp exactly, but expecting to be. Small shoots rose tentatively from the earth in the way of things that had been waiting for permission. The farther he walked, the more the land seemed to breathe, quietly and without fanfare, as though it had been holding its breath for a very long time and had only just decided to stop.
^He passed a tree stump half-buried in a slope, its spiral scar overgrown with moss.
^The spiral was unmistakable, the same shape he had traced in the dream corridor, the same one that lived on his palm.
stump_reach: ^His palm was moving before he'd stood fully upright.

^Not a decision. An understanding the body had arrived at first and was acting on without filing the paperwork. He'd been letting it do this since the ash plain, with the working theory that it had better records than he did, and the theory had not yet been disproved. The wood was warm before his fingers arrived. He registered this and pressed on anyway, in the same way he'd registered that the dream corridor had stars and kept walking.
^The glyph on his palm pulsed once in response: not pain, not heat, but the sensation of a question that had just recognized its answer from across a significant distance of time.
stump_study: ^The spiral was unmistakable, the same shape that lived on his palm, the same geometry he'd traced in the dream. He wanted to be sure he understood what he was looking at before he touched it. This felt important in the particular way that things felt important when you had no framework for them: not rationally, but with the body's insistence. The carving was deep, worn at the edges by something softer than weather, and something had grown into the cuts that held the warmth of the wood rather than the temperature of the air. He traced the outer curve with his eyes. Then the inner. Then the place where they met.
^Then he pressed his palm flat against the surface.
^The glyph pulsed once in response: not pain, not heat, but the sensation of a question that had just recognized its answer from across a significant distance of time.
after_stump: ^For one moment, just one, something moved through him. The impression of a place, enormous and patient, waiting just beyond the shape of the visible world. The feeling of a door that had been locked for a very long time, from the inside, by someone who intended to come back.

^The hills ahead had changed. Not physically, they hadn't moved. But a gap he hadn't seen before had revealed itself between them, as though the landscape had simply shifted its weight and shown him what it had been standing in front of.
^At first, he thought it was light.
^Only after all three did it resolve into form.

^The city rose without angles, curved towers of pale stone spiraling upward like something that had grown rather than been built, their surfaces etched with glyphs that moved at the edges of visibility. Bridges draped between them in wide arcs. Water fell in ribbons between the towers and scattered the sky into colors he didn't have names for. The air carried a frequency, not a sound exactly, but the feeling of a room where something important had recently happened and wasn't finished happening yet.
^He stood at the hills' edge for a long time.

^The threshold was a ring of low stone set into the earth, marked with spirals so deeply carved they seemed to shift when he looked at them sideways. Not physically. In meaning. The way certain things moved when you weren't watching them directly.
^Mist hovered just beyond the ring. He stopped at its edge.

^The spirals under him glimmered, then one faltered. Just for a heartbeat. A single line in the pattern misaligned, like a note that almost found harmony, then slipped. It corrected itself immediately. But the feeling remained.

^The glyph on his palm had gone warm, not urgently, just present, the way a familiar weight was present when you picked it up after a long time away. He stood at the threshold and felt a question that had already been answered, waiting for him to catch up to it.

^A low tone thrummed beneath him, deep and slow and ancient. It rose through his boots, his knees, his spine, and settled somewhere below his ribs in the exact location the hollow had been. Not just noticing it. Acknowledging it. Two things recognizing each other across a significant distance of time.
^At his feet, a violet bloom unfurled from between the stones.
^He looked at it for a moment.
^Then he looked up at the city and let it look back.
^He walked without direction, which seemed to be what the city wanted.
^He turned into a narrower street without deciding to, the street offered itself and his feet accepted before the rest of him was consulted.

^The buildings here were older, not in the obvious sense of deterioration — nothing in this city seemed to deteriorate so much as deepen — but in the way stone held cold, holding the memory of many seasons in its composition. The glyphs carved into these walls were larger and less decorative. More necessary. The kind of marks made not for beauty but for precision, by someone who needed the thing recorded and was not certain they would be there to record it again.

^A stretch of wall to his left had been written on. Not carved, written, in something dark that had dried to the color of old iron. He moved closer to be sure of the difference between letters and symbols, and found the distinction harder to make than expected. Whatever language this was had not separated the two.

^He stood there for a moment, aware that he was not supposed to be able to read it and also aware that something in him was trying anyway, reaching the way his hand had reached for the charcoal, before the deciding. He noticed the reaching and let it settle back, soft rather than focused, the way you looked at things in low light that sometimes sharpened when you looked slightly past them. He stood with his hands at his sides and his focus soft against the wall, and waited to see what he was about to almost understand.
^The marks held their shape. He held his.

^Not physically. Not with sound or light. The way a face shifted when you finally understood its expression, the arrangement unchanged, the meaning suddenly present. One cluster separated itself from the others and became, briefly and without explanation, something he almost knew. Not a word. The shape of one. The impression a word left in the space where it had been spoken often enough that the air remembered the gesture.
^He knew it. In the same way he knew the hollow in his chest and the glyph on his palm and the six words his hand had written before he had decided to write them.
^Then the meaning fell out of it, the way meaning sometimes left a word if you looked at it too long, and the marks were only marks, and the wall was a wall, and the street was a street.
^He looked at his palm. The glyph was warm. Not new warmth. The warmth of something that had recognized something else.
^The pool was tucked into a courtyard he found by accident, or by the streets finding it for him, the distinction, he was beginning to understand, might not exist here.

^It was perfectly still. Its surface didn't so much reflect the towers above as contain them, the image too precise to be a reflection, more like a window to a version of the city that had figured something out.
^He crouched beside it. The glyph on his palm had gone quiet.
^Then, not outward. Inward. A movement in the pool's depths, something surfacing slowly from underneath the image.

^The letters didn't glow. They resonated, each one a slightly different tone, the whole thing a chord he felt in his chest rather than heard in his ears. As he looked, the violet ink on the tips of his fingers faded, just for a moment, just long enough to see the skin beneath, clean and unstained, before it returned. The name wasn't being given to him. It was the character of the six words in the hollow, of the spiral on the stump. Old information that had finally found its way back.
pool_say: ^He said it before he'd decided to. The sound of it in the air was different from the sight of it in the water — both true, differently. The spoken version had breath in it, had weight, had the particular quality of something that now existed in more than one place at once. He sat with the shape of the name in his mouth for a moment after it was gone, the way you sat with a note after it finished sounding, checking whether the room had changed.
^The pool stilled. The name was absorbed.
pool_hold: ^He looked at it for a long time.

^It wasn't that he didn't believe it. He believed it the way he believed the hollow in his chest and the glyph on his palm: not through evidence, through the specific sensation of something finding the space that had been waiting for it. He just wanted to hold it here, in the pool's stillness, before it became something he'd said aloud and made real in the particular way that spoken things became real — committed to the air, gone from the water. He wasn't sure what the difference was. He suspected it mattered anyway.
^The pool stilled. The name was absorbed.
after_pool: ^Then the images came, brief, without order. A hall of spiraled stone, light running through the carvings like a current. Hands pressing to curved walls as tones rang out in layered harmony. A group of figures at an archway with their heads bowed in something that looked like shared vow. And beneath all of it, a feeling that wasn't memory so much as direction: toward.
^He was crouching beside a still pool in a city he didn't know, with a name that felt like coming home to a house he'd never been inside.
^"You're late," said a voice from the mist behind him.

^The figure stood in an archway beyond the pool. A staff rested against one shoulder. Their robe was the color of ink under moonlight. Their expression was that of someone who had watched a particular thing happen before and had stopped being surprised by it.
^"Not yet," they said. "But the city does."

^They turned and began to walk. He followed, because there wasn't a better option, and because the voice, dry and ancient and slightly resigned, made him want to know what exactly it was resigned about.
^The figure walked without speaking, not unfriendly, more like someone who had learned long ago that most of the things worth saying couldn't be said yet.

^They passed under an arch of pearlescent stone. Vines pulsed slowly along the walls, more like the glow of things that remembered warmth and were keeping it than any light source he could name. A bridge appeared ahead, woven from threads of translucent material that had no obvious structural right to be holding anyone up.
^The figure walked onto it without slowing.
bridge_reason: ^He stood at the edge and assessed the situation with the information available, which was: the threads had no obvious structural right to hold anyone. The figure had walked onto the bridge without slowing, which suggested confidence, or long familiarity, or some third quality he didn't have a word for. The alternative was staying on this side alone. He had been making decisions for bad reasons since the ash plain and the decisions had consistently led somewhere, which was better than nowhere.
^He put his foot on the bridge.
^It held. Each step felt like walking across a chord at the edge of recognition, one he almost knew how to hum.
bridge_step: ^He stood at the edge for approximately three seconds. The drop through the threads was visible, which he noted, and then looked away from, which was more useful. The figure was already several paces ahead and not looking back. Aerin looked down once — a mistake, in retrospect — and then looked forward, which was better.

^He wasn't sure he'd decided to. His foot had made the next move, the way his body had been making next moves since the ash plain, with the quiet authority of something that remembered this led somewhere. He let it lead. The bridge held his weight with the particular steadiness of something that had been doing this for a very long time and saw no reason to stop now.
after_bridge: ^"It won't drop you," the figure said, without turning.
^The words were too heavy for the conversation. They arrived with the weight of something much older than a bridge, a sudden jagged piece of history where there should have been only reassurance.
^Aerin looked at the back of the ink-colored robes. "In how long?"
^The figure didn't answer. He didn't turn. He simply kept walking, the staff striking the stone in a rhythm that was suddenly, pointedly, a command to follow.
^They passed through a plaza where small motes of light drifted upward from the ground, slow and without urgency. He stopped and watched one rise until it was gone.
^"The forgetting," the figure said, still walking. "Same as everywhere. Solrien simply refused to forget quietly."
^A click landed inside him, like a latch turning. He paused, the shape of something almost there and not yet reachable, then walked on.

^The map room made itself known before they reached it, the air shifting, a pressure change that set against his teeth. The figure pushed open a door that wasn't there and then was, and stepped through.

^The room was round. Twelve pillars rose from the floor in a spiral pattern, each one carved with glyphs. The floor between them was etched with layered lines, intersecting and curved and too complex to follow. And above the pillars, suspended in the air:

^The alive ones hummed at different frequencies, some bright and certain, others thin and searching, each one its own particular kind of presence. The seven dark ones gave off nothing at all. Not even the impression of absence. Just silence, the kind that came from something that had stopped rather than something that had never begun.

^"The Anchor Points," they said, in the tone of someone who had said this before under very different circumstances and hadn't decided yet how to feel about saying it again. They gestured at the five dark nodes.
^Aerin stepped forward. The glyph beneath his boot brightened. One of the living nodes pulsed once in response.
^Aerin pointed to one of the outer nodes, faint, barely there, its tone less a sound than an intention. "That one. What's wrong with it?"
^The figure's expression shifted in some small way he couldn't name. "It still remembers what it is," they said. "But not who."
^Before he could ask what that meant:
^A ping. Clear and deliberate, like someone had flicked a crystal goblet with precisely the wrong kind of confidence.
^"I touched nothing," said a voice from somewhere above them. "Except that one thing. Which hummed. But only judgmentally."
^A blur resolved itself into something beside his shoulder.

^Wings present at the shoulders, the feathers catching light in a way light didn't usually agree to, in the specific way of something that had never once needed to flap them and saw no reason to start.
^"Hello," said the blur. "I'm simply here in a resonant capacity. Don't mind me; I'm practically furniture, only with better tailoring and significantly more opinions."
^Something copper-and-bone spun between their fingers, too small to be the source of the warmth it gave the room, and did not stop spinning.
^"I'm Thistle," said the figure, in the tone of a person identifying a weather phenomenon.

^"Hi." Brightly. "Lovely chamber. Very opinionated architecture." A pause, and then, more quietly, with the energy of someone processing new information: "Oh stars, it's still vibrating. I think I may have accidentally married a resonance node."
^"In my defense, it was very forward."

^"Nothing. I was merely near the node in a way that became conversational." They turned to Aerin with the energy of something that had decided its best option was delight. "You're new. Your field is vibrating like a startled frog in a tuning fork. Genuinely it's a bit loud. Did no one warn you about entering Solrien with zero tonal discipline?"
^"I woke up in ash this morning," Aerin said. "So no."
^"Perfect." They looked back at the figure. "Elian, I'm keeping this one."
^The figure — Elian, apparently — closed their eyes briefly. "What are you doing here?"

^"Sightseeing. Possibly preventing a harmonic incident. Jury's out." Thistle turned to Aerin again. "He's very stingy with explanations," they said, of Elian, in a not-quite-whisper. "He believes the withholding is the teaching. I find it charming."
^Elian turned toward a doorway that had been doing its best not to exist. "The Archive," he said. "Since you're here." This last at Thistle, who was already moving.
^The Hall of Crossed Threads did not look like a library.

^It looked like a cathedral that had given up on ceilings and decided to think upward instead, balconies curving toward a sky it was attempting to become, vines of living ink on the walls, hovering scrolls casting their own small shadows. Threads of faint light drifted between surfaces, tugged by something that wasn't wind.
^Aerin understood, within approximately thirty seconds, that the books had opinions.
^Not metaphorically. The first one he reached for turned its spine away. The second opened and then exploded in a cloud of violet ink.
^He stood with his arms still extended, ink dripping from his chin, his shirt now the approximate color of a bruised sky. The air smelled of ozone and something that might have been mild contempt.
^Thistle, from four feet away, regarded him with the expression of a person experiencing private vindication at a calibrated distance.
^"I thought you'd figure it out faster." A tilt of the head. "You did not."
^Elian, from across the room, didn't look up from the shelf he was examining. "The ink will fade," he said. "In approximately three days."
^"It's judgmental ink. It has a sense of proportion."

^Aerin wiped his face with his sleeve. His sleeve was also now violet. He looked up at the shelves spiraling toward the ceiling, at the scrolls crossing and recrossing in the air above him, at the glass discs flickering with moving sigils and the threads of light drifting between everything with the patient purpose of something that had been doing this for a very long time.

^He understood, with the particular clarity that sometimes followed embarrassment, that he had made an error in method rather than intention. He had reached. The Archive had opinions about reaching. These two facts were not complicated in isolation. He'd simply failed to apply the lesson before it applied itself to his face.
^He tried a different approach. He stopped reaching. He simply stood, and looked, and let the room be what it was without asking anything of it.
^A scroll drifted close. Stopped near his shoulder. Then drifted on.
^The room, for its part, remained neutral on the subject of whether he had taken too long to arrive at this.
^Thistle, floating upside down near the ceiling, examined the ink-explosion book with forensic attention. "Seven out of ten for splatter," they announced. "Committed. I respect it."
^Aerin looked at Elian. "Are they always like this?"
^"There is no always with Thistle," Elian said. "There is only currently."

^He moved toward a plinth near the center of the room, where a spiral of golden thread hovered in place, slowly unwinding and rewinding, patient and purposeful, as though it had been doing this since before anything else in the room existed.
^"The Archive doesn't show what you want," Elian said, quietly. "It shows what you're ready to receive."
^"And what am I ready to receive?"
^Elian looked at him for a moment, then gave the question the weight it deserved.
^"More than you were yesterday," he said. "Less than you'll need tomorrow."

^Something in the walls, or below the walls, below the stone itself, shifted. A pressure, wordless, arriving through more channels than the ears. The hollow beneath Aerin's ribs hummed once, faintly, in the same register as whatever had just spoken.
^"It said more tonight than it has in some time," Elian observed. He moved toward the exit. "Come. The city will want quiet."
^"Solrien doesn't need quiet," Elian said. "It becomes still in a way that requires more from you than noise would."

^The room he was given was round, its walls faintly spiraling, its single arch open to a sky he had no word for. The light coming through it was the pale gold of late afternoon, but the shadows it cast on the floor belonged to a different hour entirely, longer and leaning in a direction the sun had not yet reached. As though the room remembered a previous evening and was still in it.
^He stood in the center of it for a moment.

^He looked at his hands. His ink-stained, violet, ridiculous hands. He had arrived in a city made of memory, found his own name in a pool, chosen to walk across a bridge that had decided to hold him, and been assessed by a room that had no interest in his intentions. His shirt was ruined. His face was violet. He had a glyph on his palm that kept responding to things and a hollow in his chest that had been there since he woke and a name that felt like a key he wasn't sure he had found the right lock for yet.
^It shifted under him, the way furniture shifted when it remembered a particular weight and was recalibrating.
^He lay back and stared at the ceiling until its slow spiral became something he could breathe in rhythm with.

^Somewhere below, water moved through the canals, not with the sound of running water but with the sound of something that had been running for a very long time and had stopped needing to hurry. Glyphs pulsed in the walls. The shimmer drifted in the corner like something that had followed him home and didn't have anywhere else to be.
^He put a hand over his chest, where the hollow was.
^But different. Less like absence. More like a space that had been told someone was coming.
